to grow hemp at the various experimental farms and some retting was done at the Central farm to preserve the continuity of the experiments looking toward the establishment of an industry. In view of the amount of cordage and twine we have to import and the facility with which we can grow raw material, anything we can do to promote that industry certainly deserves our attention.
Would the minister be disposed to support an increase in the bounty for next year?
It runs, I think, from year to year.
On a gradually decreasing scale.
Yes, gradually decreasing to almost zero. It starts at a cent and a half and reduces by a quarter of a cent until it disappears.

One of our good friends to the left said during the afternoon that poultry raising did not pay in Saskatchewan.
I presume he included with that poultry products. What is the experience on the experimental farms with regard to whether or not poultry pays in Saskatchewan and elsewhere?

Poultry has developed into one of the most profitable branches of farming, not only here but in other parts of Canada. During the last two years Saskatchewan has become the second largest shipper of poultry and poultry products in the Dominion, Ontario being first. In the United States the egg crop alone is worth more than the entire wheat crop of that country, showing the wonderful strides being taken in the poultry industry not only here but over the entire continent. Wherever there are facilities for taking care of the flocks, farmers and fanciers have found poultry raising very profitable. In the pioneer days the man who had not a basket of eggs and a tub of butter had very little to rely on, and now there is a good cash market for these products.

I do not want to permit the minister to forget this chilled and frozen meat business. I am not entirely surprised that the trial shipment made last summer was not a success. Imagine a new country starting grain growing and trying to put on the European market a trial shipment of grain without up-to-date elevators, without boats properly fitted, without proper

facilities at the other end. I can quite conceive of business of that kind being handled at a distinct loss. When we ship live cattle over to the Old Country there are proper facilities for handling them and for putting them on the market, but as I understand the situation the facilities with regard to chilled and frozen meat are all owned and controlled by United States packers If we sell through them, naturally they are going to see that we do not make anything out of it. This is one of the most serious conditions that we have to face to-day, and I hope the minister will give the matter more attention and not drop it at this juncture. Perhaps he could give*us some information as to this particular shipment; how it was marketed in the Old Country-because I think that is the big problem-to whom it was sold, and whether the shipments were traced right to the actual buyer. I have read that trial shipments of that kind were sold to small dealers who did not have proper facilities for keeping chilled meat. They would lose a large percentage of it and could only handle it if they allowed in the price for considerable loss. If the minister could give us some information along this line I think it would be of interest to the committee.

In anticipation of this matter creating a great deal of interest we issued a bulletin dealing with this shipment in detail, and I shall be glad to provide my hon. friend with a copy, because it goes into it much more exhaustively than I could.
With regard to the disposition of the meat in the Old Country we disposed of it under the most favourable conditions possible. We went on the ordinary produce exchanges and the butchers from the whole countryside were bidding for that meat in competition with the meat from other countries. We had this meat in the hands of a man who knew the business acting on our behalf to see that we got the last cent for it. I am not surprised that my hon. friend should wonder if every detail was properly looked after, because I must admit I was astonished at the difference in value of these animals when sold alive and as chilled meat. But here is a point that must be apparent to all. When you arrive with chilled meat on the British market it will be from twelve to fourteen days old, and you have to sell it very quickly whether there is a bidder or not, because it is in such a condition you are not able to keep it much longer. You have either to sell it or freeze it, and if you freeze it, it is in exactly the same class as the Argentine meat, and maybe not so good; so you have not the same chance of getting your price

Supply-Ayricult ure
for chilled meat as compared with the animal that is alive. If it is a steer of the proper type and breeding that goes over there, if it goes on the pasture and puts on beef rapidly, the man who buys that animal can keep it and wait for his market. He has more to say in the value of it than one has in the case of chilled beef; because if the market does not suit him, the animal is alive and can be kept, and if it is a proper animal it will get heavier and more valuable if it is kept, whereas with chilled meat you have no choice except to sell it or freeze it.
What is the difference between the price per quarter for chilled beef and fresh beef on the British market?

I have already given those figures, I think. The chilled meat by the quarter brought as close as possible to fourpence halfpenny, and the fresh meat just about twice as much as eightpence.
We have distributed a great many copies of this bulletin, which goes into the minutest possible details. We could have conducted a second shipment; in fact, it was my idea to continue to remain on the market if we had money enough for three or four months to break down the prejudice against chilled meat and demonstrate to the buying public right there, even if we lost a little money, that this was a good article. But you have some contract if you are going to undertake to educate and cultivate the taste of the United Kingdom. They had a taste long before I had, and it is far better and cheaper to try and meet their taste than to undertake to change it in regard to meat or any other product. So I felt, in view of our experience and the experience of the Harris people, who had continued their shipments for two successive years and lost S30,000 per annum in the experiment, that it was hopeless to continue, because we had just repeated their experience. I had not enough money in sight to continue, and we simply did not spend any more money on it, although we had the vote of $25,000 passed last session. We simply experimented with our own cattle, and quit after that experience.
Would not the experiment of handling only fifty carcasses be a great deal more expensive than if a much larger shipment had been made?

As a rule, volume counts, but we got a very favourable rate on this shipment. It was killed in the abattoir of the Canadian Pacific Railway in Montreal, and they gave us very favourable terms on it because they also were interested in the shipment. The shipment cost us just as much
per hundred as if it had been twice as large, and when it went on the market over there it was hung up in one or two exchanges in competition with the meat from other countries and was handled as carefully as possible, because we were naturally desirous of having it make as favourable a showing as possible, and we gave it every opportunity. The three lots were divided so as to make them as nearly uniform as possible in condition and quality. I admit that you could arrive at more definite conclusions if you could continue the shipments over a year; there is no question about that. There will be a certain amount of prejudice that you will be able to remove by the continuity of your shipments of good meat, but it would take a lot of money to do that.
Another feature I might mention is that the better the meat was the more disposed the tradesmen were to pass if off as fresh-killed meat; so there was that difficulty too. Possibly, we could not prove it but some of the best of it was no doubt sold in that way. You know how these things goj the better it is the more tendency there is to palm it off as fresh-killed meat after the tradesmen have got it, but not when they are buying it.
In reply to my hon. friend's question, the meat sold for 4s. 2jd. per stone, or 124 cents per pound, for the hind quarter, and 2s. OJd. per stone for the fore quarter. I was more disappointed possibly than my hon. friend at the result of the shipment. I thought that because of the reduction in freight, and leaving all the offal here, we might make something, but we lost $7 per head on that, and that helped to offset anything we made on the other end.

I am not entirely convinced that it is a matter of educating the taste of the United Kingdom, because the figures prove they are consuming enormous quantities of chilled meat to-day. I was glad to hear the minister refer to the possibility of some of this chilled meat having been sold as fresh meat, for that is just what I have heard. I understand that a good deal of the chilled meat was sold in that way. The figures here show that 5,076,000 British hundredweight-of 112 pounds-of chilled meat were imported and consumed in the Old Country in 1923.
I am glad to hear that the minister has issued a bulletin that will give us some information with respect to this shipment, but I am not entirely convinced that it is impossible for us to get some of this trade. I think the matter is worthy of further study, although perhaps not to the extent of wasting any
Supply-Agriculture

considerable amount of money on it. I think we should study the possibilities of this trade very carefully. If they are able to ship large quantities from the Argentine-and they are doing this repeatedly as the figures show-I see no reason why we should not be able to do it in. Canada. If there is anything lacking it probably has to do with facilities. The Argentine has the proper facilities for handling this trade. The large American packers who are making imports into England from the Argentine have their facilities already established and built up, and my opinion is that we must use the same kind of facilities to meet our competitors in that market. I am not sure whether that is correct or not, but it seems to me it is a point well worth looking into.

If my hon. friend, or any other hon. gentleman would like to try the experiment over again we can carry it out this year with our own cattle, I mean the experimental farm cattle. If my hon. friend would care to discuss the matter further with me I shall be quite willing to hear him. There seems to be a general feeling in favour of repeating this experiment, and we shall be in a position to do so. We shall havb a lot of first class stuff ready for shipment in the course of another month or so. There is a bunch up at Rosthern that I think are exceedingly good, and there are some at the Central farm in the same category. We will make inquiries in the meantime just to see if we slipped a cog anywhere in the last experiment. If there is we shall try not to repeat the mistake. We do not like to lose $50 a steer on these farm steers; it makes a worse showing next year when we are discussing the estimates, and the returns from that particular farm will be that much less. However, since these farms are not there primarily to make a dividend or make money directly, we Should not attach too much importance to that phase of the matter in the interests of the experimental farm. Therefore,
I will consider the advisability of making another shipment, which I am rather disposed to favour.

In connection with the chilled meat trade between Canada and the Old Country I was in England in 1921 when some private shipments were made from a Toronto abattoir to London. I accompanied the manager of the Toronto abattoir when he went down to Smithfield market for his returns, and heard his conversation with the broker down there who handled his product. At that time fresh killed beef in Great Britain was selling for about twice as much as

frozen beef or chilled beef. The broker explained the small price that he had to pay him for that chilled beef by the statement that he could not be expected to sell that meat for any more than the English butcher would pay for it. It did not make any difference whether the meat came from Canada or the Argentine. If it had been put in cold storage that settled it; it was all treated as chilled or frozen beef and would only sell for the lower price. These experiments were carried on by private enterprise, as we have already said, Sir, and a loss of $36,000 per year was sustained as stated by the minister. While the government's intentions were quite good in this matter if there is any criticism I have to offer it would be that they undertook this venture with the full knowledge that it had failed already in private hands, for after all private enterprise must make the real experiment in any undertakings of the kind. From all I can learn there is no use in our endeavouring to compete with the Argentine under present conditions in the chilled beef market in London, for the reason that with their very mild climate and their low prices for labour they are able to put meat on the market at a profit for a very much lower price than Canadians can.
With regard to the experimental farm system in general, I want to say that having looked into the matter pretty well, and having an opportunity of doing so, I feel, that we have perhaps, one of the very best experimental farm systems in the world. I have heard Old Country people remark on this, visitors who were enthusiastic over what we have here. I have visited farms in Great Britain and I think there is nothing-so far as I was able to discover at least-that would compare with the Central Experimental Farm in Ottawa. If there is one thing wrong with the experimental farm system of Canada it is that the people who should use that system do not do so to anything like a sufficient degree.
With reference to the depots for breeding pure bred stock, so long as you only have the herds that are necessary to carry on your experimental work no reasonable objection can arise. But when it comes to increasing your herds to an unusual degree it produces the competition that is going to be felt by the general breeders of the country. What the minister said about selling a pure bred animal on the frontier and in this way creating an interest in pure bred stock and stimulating a market is doubtless correct. Any pure bred animal going out on the same frontier, whether produced at the experimental

Supply-Agriculture
farms or by a private breeder will have the same effect. In the province of British Columbia we have perhaps one of the most up-to-date establishments to be found anywhere in Canada in the Colony farm. There we find that the government has a good many advantages in the way of advertising. They are able to distribute their information, the information reaches the breeders and the buyers coming into the country, and their natural inclination is to buy from a government farm simply because the purchase will have the government guarantee behind it. With few exceptions the government is able to make a much better display at exhibitions and to sell at a more reasonable price than the breeder. At the same time the system cannot be unduly extended without competing and interfering with the legitimate breeder.

I quite agree with what has been said by the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) with respect to breeding depots.
I think only such numbers of stock should be kept on these farms as are necessary for experimental work. I do not agree with the last speaker, however, that the breeders would fear competition from the experimental farms, because we have been given to understand that the labour costs at these farms are three or four times more than they are at the institutions of private breeders. I rather imagine that the experimental farms would suffer from competition with the private breeders.
There is something in that.

I believe that these breeding depots would produce at a loss and being desirous of making the best possible expenditure of public money I should not be in favour of using the farms for that purpose. I should like to draw the attention of the minister to another point and that is I believe the animals kept at an experimental farm should be of the types that are popular in the district. For instance, in Quebec there is a certain breed of dairy cattle that are very popular, and it is only proper that the stations in that province should emphasize the importance of that particular breed. If shorthorn cattle are popular in a particular district let the experimental farm concentrate on shorthorn cattle. And so throughout the whole of Canada. I believe that in that way you would have cattle that would be more useful for exhibiting the advantages of breeding, and you would have herds that would be more useful to the community to be served. Furthermore they could produce, not at a loss, but on a basis that would be profitable to the country.

In the early part of
his remarks this afternoon, the minister spoke about breeding and distribution stations. I would like to go into a discussion of that matter, but I think, looking at the items further down, that it might properly come under some other head than that of experimental farms. However, it has been touched on and if the minister would prefer that the discussion should go on under this item I am prepared to proceed. If not, I will drop it now and discuss it later.

This is the proper
item under which to discuss it.

In view of the remarks of some of my colleagues, I have no doubt they will not agree with what I have to suggest. The hon. minister will remember that last fall, during his visit to the West, he was waited on in the city of Winnipeg by a group of gentlemen interested in developing new industries, particularly in Manitoba. In sections of that province, as the hon. minister is well aware, the people have come to the stage in farming operations where it will be necessary for them to make somewhat of a change. The change which is most highly recommended for those people to adopt is that of dairying. In order to go into that branch of farming they must have dairy cattle. We have no great supply of dairy cattle in western Canada. The people need these cattle now, and some of the gentlemen interested in the development of that industry made it their business to inquire where suitable dairy stock could be secured, and I think it was brought to the attention of the minister, at the meeting to which I refer, that stock of that kind could be secured at very desirable prices in the state of Wisconsin. If I am correctly informed, the minister was asked if he thought it would be desirable to have the duty removed, or the arrangement suspended, so that the duty would not be collected on a certain number of high-class dairy cattle if they were brought into that particular section of the country. I am informed that he looked upon that scheme rather favourably at the time, and agreed to take up the matter when he came back to Ottawa. I understand that he further agreed to send representatives of his department into Wisconsin to inquire into conditions there. Has that been done? If it has, who went, and what was the result? If the result was favourable to reduction in the duty, or the elimination of the duty altogether, those people might get their cattle from the nearest market and the cheapest market from which they could be supplied for that section of the country. I understand

Supply-A griculture

that it has been stated there is a plentiful supply of that class of stock in eastern Canada. My hon. friend will be interested in this statement. However, I am quite sure that, being opposed to protection of any nature, he would not object to the people in Manitoba-especially in the southern part of Manitoba where conditions are such that it is absolutely necessary that some other branch of the agricultural industry must be taken up with grain growing-purchasing their dairy stock in the cheapest market they can find. If the time ever comes when that particular locality becomes a dairy district, I will be an anti-protectionist even to the extent of oleomargarine. I think we should have free trade in that line. In fact, I think the minister knows that it is absolutely necessary that the people in that part of the country should not only procure their dairy stock as cheaply as possible but that they should be permitted to buy wherever they can make the purchase.

The hon. Minister of Agriculture has received a very great deal of advice this afternoon, but I hope that the little bit I have to add to that already given will be patiently borne by him. We have sat all afternoon and all evening until the present hour discussing quite seriously the experimental farms, and yet in the opinion of the average farmer of Canada the experimental farms, if alluded to or thought of, are always mentioned with a sort of righteous contempt. I think that possibly the reason why the average farmer has very little to say for the experimental farm is that the experimental farms have never been made to pay, they have never put in practice the 'lesson they have tried to teach the farmers. It seems that it is easier for them to give advice than to carry their own teachings into practice. The experimental farms have drummed, and drummed, and drummed, on production. But our difficulty now is not a lack of production, but over-production and lack of marketing facilities. The difficulty the farmer experiences is in getting a just proportion of the selling price of his goods. The sellipg price of his goods is not high enough to pay him for producing those goods. I remember a suggestion that, I believe, was made in the House last year,-and I certainly heard the matter talked about outside of the House by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland)-that the strictly experimental work should come under the Industrial Research department, and the parks and all the beautiful picnic grounds should be under the Parks department, where they naturally belong. I 
would advise the hon. gentleman (Mr. Motherwell) to cut out the frills and the picnics. I never go out to the experimental farm in Ottawa, with all its beauty, without coming home raging angry, I think about the people who pay for that farm, who have not one shrub around their house, who have no bulbs, who have no beauty, who have not much enjoyment in life, because of the foolish things that are imposed upon them by governments, not only of the Dominion but of the provinces, counties and townships. I think, if this work of experimental farms is to go on those farms will have to turn their attention to the science of marketing farm products and not to the producing of more goods. If they would meet, without political bias, the voluntary organizations of farmers, and assist them to market their products efficiently and well, they would be doing a real service to Canada. But no, they will sit back and wait till the farmer himself, loaded down with all his handicaps, has solved his own problem, and then will come along with theories for co-operative marketing. But in this criticism I must remember to praise the federal Department of Agriculture for one thing,-they have begun co-operative marketing of eggs and have assisted the farmers in many places to get an idea of how these things should be done. If they would carry out that idea in other branches of marketing farm products, it would be very much better.
I think that this item has been discussed, not only long enough but too long. We have wasted a lot of money talking about it, and I think the minister has forgotten nfost of what we have said, and he should, if he wishes to retain his faculties. I, therefore, move:
That item No. 40 of the Agricultural Estimates be reduced by $200,000.

Before the vote is
taken, I should like to answer a question put by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Steedsman). His recital of the circumstances in connection with the desire to import dairy cattle from the United States is substantially correct. When I was in Manitoba, I met a large deputation in Premier Bracken's office by appointment. This deputation represented the railways, the newspapers, the milk producers and several other parties, and they asked me to use my endeavours, when I came back to Ottawa, to have high-class, grade dairy cattle, permitted to enter Canada the same as pure bred cattle. I naturally was in sympathy with this idea, particularly as I knew that the people of Manitoba were

Supply-Agricult ure
ready to go into dairying and needed this so badly. But I have my limitations, especially as regards a reduction in tariffs when the House is not in session, and nothing could be done that I could see. I made inquiries into the matter, and I found that there was no such thing as a certificate of a grade animal. You have to have some way of indicating whether an animal is pure bred or not and this is done by a certificate. There is no request that, from a personal standpoint, I would have liked more to meet, especially in view of the peculiar situation of Manitoba at this time. I may say that this is a matter which we can deal with, if we like, in the coming budget. Shall we remove the duty from American farm animals, particularly dairy cattle, regardless of what they do with ours? I am hopeful that before very long our cattle will be received very much more favourably in the American market, but I do not know whether that day will be hastened by our giving away our part of the contract by letting American animals in first. I have some misgivings in that regard, although I am not a stickler on it. Sometimes things become so bad that you have to adopt a certain course regardless of what the other fellow does. We have the same suggestion as regards breeding ewes and lambs. The problem is a big one to know what you should do with regard to American grade stock. I might, however, point out that I was quite unable, as the whole cabinet would be unable, to do anything by order in council between sessions, and now that parliament has assembled, there is an embargo against these animals because of the outbreak of the foot-and-mouth disease in the United States. That trouble may disappear, although the disease is beginning to spread very seriously. Under present conditions, however, the problem is not capable of immediate solution.
As regards the question of investigation, I sent a competent man to Wisconsin to inquire, first, into the quality of these cattle. It was represented that you could get animals with a production of from eight to ten thousand pounds a year for a comparatively reasonable amount, running from $100 to $125 a head. My experience in life has taught me that very rarely anybody wants to sell a cow of that character. Although such cows are quite common, at the same time they are much better than the average cow and very few dairymen want to sell them. If you want to buy them, you have to give the man his price, and it is generally a good 52i
price. Our man came back and reported, and, anticipating this discussion, I have his report here. I will summarize it rather than read it. He visited Wisconsin; he visited the herds, and found that freight rates were actually not as good from Wisconsin to Manitoba as from here, because of the reduced rates given by both railways to this class of stock for transportation to the West. As regards the cattle, he found that there were no better buys in Wisconsin than in the older provinces of Canada. I noticed a report by a representative of the Milk Producers' Association-I forget the gentleman's name-who reports the very opposite. He insists that there are better purchases in Wisconsin; that you can get a bettter cow for $100 in Wisconsin than you can here. He does not say anything about freight rates being less favourable there than here. The result is that whichever report you like, you have your choice. In our report there is no desire to represent anything but the actual facts as Mr. Cook found them. He is a man well versed in freight rates and also in cattle, so he was in a good position to size the matter up. His report is too long to read; but let us say that the matter is in doubt inasmuch as our representative and the representative of the Milk Producers' Association report differently.
There is another way of starting dairying, a way that is being taught by an expert that I know of on this continent, particularly when a poor man wants to start. The idea is to begin with such animals as are within reach, of the particular type you want for breeding or milk. Buy those females, then endeavour to get a good male at the head of your herd, and breed up into something better. That may take too long, but at the same time it is not by plunging into something that is expensive that we are going to get on our feet in western Canada. Getting out of one hole to crawl into another very rarely succeeds. In the Winnipeg market, you will find you can buy five dairy type heifers for the same price that you would give for one Ontario or one Wisconsin cow. As regards freight rates, the government pays 75 per cent of the freight rates on these young females or any other live stock into the West; the railways pay 25 per cent; and the hotel bills of the buyers are also paid by the government so that you can go on to the Winnipeg market, the Calgary market, the Prince Albert market, buy an animal and ship it back into the interior without paying one dollar of transportation for the animal or the man. In view of that, I feel very strong-
Supply-A griculture

ly that a man who wants to start dairying can start in that way more cheaply and safely, particularly if a group of farmers organize, take the opportunity of forming a cattle association, and get for that particular district a male that will mate with those heifers. That is the way every experimental farm demonstrates as the most successful. The other way is to buy high-bred, expensive cattle in a southern country, where there are all kinds of modern facilities for housing the animals, where there is either good hay or good ensilage to feed them, and bring them up into a more northern climate and into the average facilities that we have for taking care of them. You will soon convert a ten-thousand-pound cow into a four-thousand-pound cow, and before you know where you are, your investment is reduced by more than 50 per cent. I am not putting this up for the purpose of giving some alternative; but the fact remains that, because of the embargo, we could not import those cattle, even if the duty were removed. We always have the other avenue available in order to start in dairying, and in my estimation those who have made the most pronounced success in dairying have started in that more modest way and have grown up in that business. I see the hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. Warner) who is recognized as an authority on dairying. I have never discussed this phase of the question with him, but I feel satisfied that his general experience running over a great many years will enable him to substantiate what I have said. All the experimental farms that we have, whether you find one at Nappan or at Agassiz, show that the proper way for a man with limited means to raise a dairy herd is to start on a modest scale with the females, as I have described. When the budget comes down I think we shall find that owing to the exigencies of the country's financial situation it will be impossible for every one to have the duties reduced to the extent that he would wish.

I want to add a few words to what has been said by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Steedsman) with regard to dairy cattle. The minister referred to the fact that a gentleman had been sent out to make an investigation in Wisconsin in connection with the dairy business, and there is no doubt that the Winnipeg District Milk Producers' Co-operative Association were not by any means satisfied with the disclosures he made in his report. The gentleman referred to by the minister is Mr. Tovell, who,
I may say, is thoroughly well informed on 
all matters appertaining to the dairy business and is therefore competent to carry on the investigational work which he undertook. I am informed that he was sent out by the provincial government, in co-operation, I presume, with the Winnipeg District Milk 1 roducers Association. His report is most emphatic in support of the statement that has been made that large numbers of dairy cows can be purchased in Wisconsin and Minnesota at prices that would make their importation into Manitoba profitable if it were not for the duty. His report takes cognizance of the freight rates. Mr. Tovell also emphasizes the fact that the people of Wisconsin and Minnesota are making a special effort to cater to the trade of producing daily cows, of which large numbers are available. Part of the report includes a map covering a number of counties in which, are marked the number of dairy cows that are available, and in no instance as any county shown with a smaller number than 10,000. I see by the map that in some cases they run as high as 45,000. The minister is of the opinion that the best way to begin dairying is to buy a few heifers at the Winnipeg stock yards. I doubt the wisdom of this suggestion. It is true, perhaps, that you can begin cheaper that way, but I am satisfied that if a man is able at all to begin by buying a few first-class cows which he knows to be good, which have been tested and have a production record, or which have come from cows that have borne such a record, it would be much more satisfactory in the long run. Indeed, I question very much whether there are in the Northwest a sufficient number of dairy cows to produce the young heifers for which there would be an almost immediate demand, and I would urge strongly that the government make a note of these facts. I would seriously suggest that consideration be given to the request that these dairy cows should be admitted free of duty. We are a long way from Ontario, and while we are told that we can get cattle in Ontario and Quebec and also in the Maritime provinces, at the same time, from investigation that has been made, it would seem that, from the prices for which they can foe obtained, together with 9 p.m. the high freight rate and the effect which the long rail jour-Dey has on animals, it is much more desirable to purchase the cows from the nearest point. I think the minister should give further study to the report that has been made by Mr. Tovell. He is very much interested in the dairy business and is a man who is quite competent to form an opinion on ques-

Supply-Agriculture
tions of this kind. Those of us who know him are satisfied that he is very thorough when he undertakes such an investigation as he has carried out in this instance. He conscientiously devotes his abilities to finding out all that can be ascertained about these questions, and altogether I do not know of any man who is better informed on all matters relating to dairying from one end of Canada to the other.
As regards experimental farms in general,
I believe, as the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) said, that we have a good system in Canada, and I believe that they have done splendid work in the past. It may possibly be true that in some cases, such as Indian Head, they seem for a time, I will not say to have outlived their usefulness, but to have reached that stage where it is necessary for them to devote their attention rather to some new phase of agriculture which was not perhaps recognized in the earlier days. I think, however, that we can offer this criticism, which has been urged again and again this afternoon, that there is too much overlapping; so that the Dominion department must institute a better method of co-operation with the provincial departments.
I do not think there is any question on that point. It may be that certain lines of work can best be carried on by the provinces, and others by the Dominion. I had the privilege within the last few months of visiting two of the smaller farms, one in my own constituency, situated at Morden, and I am satisfied, from what I saw there and from what I know of the character of the young man in charge of the station, that the farm is performing a splendid service to the community. There is in my constituency, as the minister is aware, the greatest fruit-growing district in the prairies. True, the work has been to a large extent developed by private enterprise, the late Mr. Stevenson having done splendidly in that direction, and the work is now being continued not only by his sons but, as well, at the experimental station. New varieties of fruit have been developed and there is, I think, every reason to believe that from the work that is being done at that station we shall be able to supply the prairies with varieties of fruit trees which, while they will not constitute a commercial industry in those provinces, will nevertheless to a large degree enable the people of the prairies to supply their own wants. That I think is quite within the realm of possibility, and anyone who has seen what is being done there to-day must have a high appreciation of this particular line of endeavour.
The late Mr. Stevenson used to produce fruit commercially.

Yes: I think it should be borne in mind particularly that the district is peculiarly fitted-perhaps it is better fitted than any other part of the prairies-for the production of apples. Some time I am going to follow the example set by the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell) and the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) and bring a sample of Manitoba apples. I also had the privilege of visiting the experimental farm at Summer-land, British Columbia. I am not quite sure that all the lines of work that are being carried on there are advisable; I had some doubts as to the experiments they were making in the feeding of cattle. However, with the small opportunity I had for investigation I would not care to pronounce positively on that point. But I was very much interested in one branch of the work. They had there a pathological laboratory in charge of a young man who seemed to be the ideal type of person for carrying on that work. He is an intense enthusiast and his investigations of diseases affecting fruit, which can be carried on only in the district in which the fruit grows, will be of untold value to fruit growers of British Columbia. We cannot afford to scoff at the work that is being done by the experimental farms. Let us take it for granted that a lot of work is done that perhaps produces no immediate results. Well, plenty of work is done that does not produce any results and that cannot be said directly to pay in dollars and cents. We cannot expect that of work that is necessarily experimental. It is possible that some lines of work might be dropped; just which I would not like to say. The farms have done good service in the past, and while some readjustments may be necessary I believe they will continue to do good work. The minister would do well to take heed of many of the suggestions made this afternoon looking to an improvement of the situation in order to make the institution meet more nearly the needs of the present day, as we are satisfied it did meet the needs in the past. The Brandon "experimental farm has rendered a splendid service to agriculture. It may be in the same position as the Indian Head farm; I rather think it is. And that it will perhaps have to branch out into lines of work which did not seem necessary in the early days. But I should regard it as a disaster if we should unduly handicap the work of those who are carrying on the activities of our experimental farms.	1

I have some pretty clear
ideas regarding these experimental farms,
Supply-Agriculture

though they may not coincide with those of some others who have spoken. In the first place, I believe there is altogether too much overlapping in this experimental work. People do not always distinguish, however, between an experimental farm and a demonstration farm. Some of the farms in Alberta were designed to demonstrate how to make fanning pay,-and in that I do not think they have succeeded as well as they might-but the experimental farm is an entirely different thing. We never expect an experimental farm to pay; you might just as well expect a laboratory in a factory to pay. It is impossible to avoid mistakes, but the mistakes that the experimental farms have made have meant more money to me than their successes. That may seem to be a queer statement, but those mistakes prevented me from doing the same thing. I have made a good many mistakes in my operations in farming and I have always found them expensive, but certainly since going to Alberta I have avoided a good many through knowing what the experimental farms have done and tried to do. I do not think the discussion here has been altogether fair; the eagerness for criticism has gone just a little too far. I have been connected with this work long enough to know something about it. I am afraid the idea is going to be held out that our experimental farms have fallen into disgrace. Personally I do not believe that that is the case. I have already admitted that I believe there has been overlapping, and perhaps there have been too many of the farms. It is a question whether we should have an experimental farm at Lacombe when there is another of the same kind at Edmonton; there is not enough variation in the climatic conditions to justify the placing of two farms so close together. But the farm at Lacombe is there, and it has been there a long while. A certain amount of experimental work is also done at the university at Edmonton. That work has been quite useful to me, as it would be to others if they would take the pains to use it. To my knowledge now varieties have been propagated through the work of the experimental farms, with resulting benefit to Canada that would be valued at thousands and even millions of dollars. I do not think that the amount of money expended is anything like as great as the value to the country of some of these experiments. We must have our experimental farms, because they are going to save the farmers a whole lot of money. They may not be carried on in the most economical or perhaps in the most intelligent way in every instance; as I have said before, 
mistakes are bound to be made. I do think that those in charge of the farms might well have assisted in working out a scheme to market the products that they were teaching the people to raise, and the Dominion Department of Agriculture could serve the people well by doing something in that line. The lefeience to chilled beef this afternoon had a bearing on that subject, and I was disappointed to hear the results of the minister's experiments with those shipments. However, when the minister got such a lick as that, and after the experience of the packing plants throughout the country, which had a very similar experience, I do not blame him for being cautious about spending more monev along that line but I would like to see this matter further investigated. I think we could do better than that. We want to learn which is the best way to ship, whether in the form of chilled meat or sending the animals over alive, and I suppose we have tried both ways to find out. That is part of the work that the Dominion Department of Agriculture ought to carry on, and their mistakes will be profitable to us because we will avoid them.
Now a word along another line. I do not know that my feelings are more highly cultivated than others along the line of beautifying our homes and so forth, but I want to tell the members of this House that I do take a whole lot of pride in some efforts I have made to beautify the surroundings of my home with trees and shrubbery, and if it had not been for the guidance of the experimental farms at Lethbridge and Lacombe,
I would have made a great many serious mistakes in planting this shrubbery. The farms have served me very well in that respect, I have heard talk about the Indian Head farm. I do not know much of its value in teaching the people in that neighbourhood how to conduct their operations, it may have outlived its usefulness in some lespects. But I know that the people in our part of the country when they want to beautify their homes go to Indian Head to get. the trees, and they are mighty glad to do it. I erhaps the farm i3 not making money out of the trees they are raising, but you cannot calculate the value of this work in dollars and cents. Go out through that country and look at the beautiful groves of trees that have been planted, and you will appreciate the value of the work that is being done at Indian Head in growing trees. I feel quite warm on this matter. I feel that it is worth talking about. I cannot imagine a young man going on a farm on the prairie and never planting a 'single shrub or tree to

beautify his home. It does not take much to do it. I have been through it; I am not talking about something I know nothing about, because I have seen the time when I was building my first home, when I did not have a dollar to buy anything with, but I got it one way or another. I took a lot of pains here and there and I did a whole lot of begging, and I did not have an experimental farm in those days to go to but I beautified my home and left it there for someone else to get the benefit of. I went to Alberta, and there I had the experimental farm to help me, and it was not nearly so expensive for me to do around my home what I had done before I came to Alberta.
As to whether the experimental farms are paying, I do not think they have paid along some lines, but they have paid just as well and perhaps a little better than some experiments that I have made myself. However, I have succeeded in growing fruit trees at my home in Edmonton. I have one tree on which I had over six hundred crabs last year. I do not ever expect to make money out of growing such things as that, but the experimental farm helped me to demonstrate that I could grow crabs in that country. When it comes down to estimating in dollars and cents the value of the work they are doing, the experimental farms are not making money very probably, and we do not need to expect that, but they are helping to make Canada a better place to live in and helping the people on the prairies to have better and nicer homes, and helping us to avoid mistakes along that line. I think the experimental farms have proved a great asset to this country. We want them carried on just as economically as possible, and we do not want any more farms than we actually need. If it would pay to close down some of the farms I am perfectly willing that the minister should do it, but I want the work they are doing to be carried on extensively in the future, in order that the people may get the benefit, and if it is costing us a little money I think it is well worth while.

I listened, because I am interested, to the discussion of the free importation of grade dairy cows. I followed the minister's words as carefully as I could, but I am afraid I was left in the same mist as at the beginning. I want to know what the minister's opinion on the subject is. For a while I thought he was against it, but towards the last he intimated that he really was not against it, but that he was waging a valiant and bloody battle inside the cabinet for it but so far not successfully. What does
the minister think on the subject? Is he in favour of it or against it? I understood he had given a judgment; indeed, I understood that he had given two. The first delegation that waited on him came away quite hopeful, not of a change in the law, but that the minister would get it done by order in council, by a change in the regulations, but subsequently they were notified that it could not be done at all. Will the minister tell us whether it ought to be done or whether it should not? He is Minister of Agriculture and a member of the government, and perhaps he can solve this question.

I was asked to permit grade dairy cattle in free. I pointed out that I had no authority to do it. I have not discussed this matter in council in full. I have discussed it with the Minister of Customs, but it has not gone any farther than that with regard to taking the duty off at that time, because we found we did not have authority to take it off. It only applied to pure bred animals. The situation now is such that you could not get them in any way if they were free, because of the embargo. If my hon. friend wants to know my personal opinion-
Is there an embargo on cattle from the United States coming into Canada?
Yes. Art thou a citizen of Canada and knowest not these things?	.
I am afraid my hon. friend's knowledge of the Scriptures is better than his knowledge of Canada. Is there an embargo on all cattle into Canada?
Yes.
Of course, there is examination, and there may be particular examination on account of the foot-and-mouth disease, but does the minister say there is an absolute embargo?

Surely. The embargo was put on first against three states because of an outbreak in California, and the two adjoining states were included in the embargo area. Consequently, if we wanted to ship to the markets of Great Britain, we had to follow suit with respect to the United States; in other words, we were compelled to put on an embargo against the United States if we wanted to retain a market for our stockers in Great Britain. I regret

It is therefore all the more imperative that we should keep that market good and tight until at least sixty days after the expiration of the last outbreak.

How long is it since
the complete embargo was put on American cattle?

It has been on
about three weeks, speaking roughly.

What was the opinion
of the minister up to three weeks ago to the admission of these animals?

My opinion was- speaking personally, I cannot speak for the cabinet that I would like to see those animals let in. At the same time I recognize there is another side to the story. I have had representations from the cattle men, the cattle growers in Manitoba vehemently objecting to it and saying "We have cattle to sell." The farmers of Manitoba and Saskatchewan say they have cattle to sell and why open the door to Wisconsin stock. That was the other side of the question. On general principles, however, speaking personally and knowing the need of Manitoba, and notwithstanding the fact that our reports indicate that when you take the freight rate into consideration, there is no better "buy" than at home, the people of that province have been under the impression that they were buying to better advantage when they bought at Wisconsin. If they are able to buy stock to advantage it means that they will go into dairying more quickly and more generally, and that is what was aimed at by the preaching of diversified farming. But if obstacles are placed in the way they say "Oh what is the use," become discouraged, and the end sought to be achieved is frustrated. Taking all things into consideration personally, as a western man, I would like to see them have access to the American market not only for dairy cattle but also for sheep anl lambs because there is considerable demand for both.
What the minister means is access from the American market?

I hesitate to take up any
time by a speech, but I feel in duty bound to say something with respect to experimental farms. I do not wish to cast any reflections on the member for Strathcona (Mr. Warner), but when he was talking about his early struggles it reminded me of a Scotch story that I am going to tell the House. An old gentleman was giving advice to his son who was going forth into the world and he wanted to put the latter right. He said, "My son, mak' money. Mak' it honestly if you can, but mak' money." I do not for a moment imagine that was how the hon. member for Strathcona got along, although doubtless he was hard pressed at the commencement of his career.
In reference to the experimental farms I believe they are doing good, useful work even to-day. In saying that, I perhaps express an opinion that differs from some hon. gentlemen sitting around me. I must confess that my knowledge of these institutions is very largely confined to the Brandon farm, but I should like to acquiesce in the statement of the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie), that the shortcoming which exists lies not so much in the farms themselves as in the fact that the farmers do not take advantage of what these institutions have to offer them. Last summer I visited the experimental farm twice. On both occasions there was a sort of picnic of farmers from the surrounding country. Addresses were given and visitors were conducted all over the farm, inspecting the different plots that were under crop. Now, as hon. members know, last year was one of the years when

Supply-Agriculture
rust inflicted very serious damage on the crops in the West. At Brandon experimental farm there were probably twenty or thirty *different varieties of wheat growing in different plots, and no better lesson as to the right sort of wheat to resist rust could be taught the farmers than was demonstrated at that farm. At the same time, I question if one-twentieth of the farmers know anything about the tests that are taking place. Of course, literature describing these tests is sent out, but I am afraid that literature is so voluminous in character that it defeats its own purpose. If the quantity of literature was less it would doubtless be more widely read.
In regard to the vegetables, and the other farm crops, I think a great deal of advantage can be gained by a visit to the farm at Brandon. The manager of that farm, Mr. McKilligan, is a farmer bora and bred, although of course he got his education at an agricultural college. But he is an enthusiast in his work and I am sure that that farm is up to date. Notwithstanding what the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) thought- maybe he did not actually say so-that it was falling behind the times, the Brandon experimental farm is an up-to-date institution and is doing good work. I want to pay a tribute to the superintendent in charge of that farm who is a good, live man and always ready to help the farmers in every way possible. Furthermore the experimental farm in Brandon has done something towards promoting co-operative marketing in eggs and poultry. I do not know whether that action is official, or otherwise, but the superintendent has taken an active part in that work and is a most energetic and praiseworthy individual.
I do not know whether the minister is entitled to all the money he is asking to carry on this work; it may be that he is asking too big a vote altogether. There was a large deputation to-day from all over the Dominion strongly urging economy, and it may be possible for the minister to get along with a little less money than he is asking for. I wanted to put myself on record on this matter. There may be too many experimental farms, but I do know that some of them are doing good work.

I had not intended saying anything on this topic but the remarks of the hon. member for Southeast drey (Miss Macphail) have brought me to my feet. In her speech to-night, referring to the Central Experimental Farm, she said she never visited that farm but she came back in a raging anger. I may say that I have never returned
from a visit to the experimental farm in that state of mind. I have visited the farm very often and have returned feeling that I had benefited by what I had seen. It would appear from the remarks of the hon. member that she is not very conversant with floriculture or horticulture. Quite a number of my constituents are interested in both and I think we should be ill-advised to vote for the reduction of the vote for experimental farms seeing the attention that is paid there to these branches of work. There may be a certain amount of overlapping but that difficulty can be cured.
I am pleased to see that the minister is putting up a larger green house at the farm and I congratulate him upon it. In such institutions the government can carry on experiments that cannot very well be undertaken by individuals. To these farms the farmers can go and obtain valuable instruction. The hon. member for Southeast Grey may sneer at the experimental farm if she chooses, but that is not the attitude adopted by the farmers in my constituency. If people are sneering, it is because they do not take advantage of what they can get by visiting the farms. Floriculture has grown in the province of Ontario to a large extent, and our horticultural societies to-day are of great benefit. I do not know any person in my constituency who is not a member of the horticultural society. We know it is a great society. It makes more beautiful homes; it makes half your home. We are told about the bulbs and shrubs at the experimental farm, and I may say to the hon. member for Southeast Grey that on application to the farm she can secure some of those without any cost. They are distributed free if you wish them, and one point that some people take exception to is that that free distribution comes in competition with the growers and dealers. But that does not occur to any great extent. My idea is that at the experimental farm we should grow the best of everything. The Department of Agriculture is in a position to buy the best of everything, and any person who visits the farm should have the opportunity of viewing the best of its kind. At some future time I should like to put on record the volume of business done even in the bulb business alone. Any person who visited the gladioli show at Guelph must have had his eyes opened. It was a wonderful show. And if we were to condemn the experimental farm, where would our Marquis wheat be? Not only the Marquis wheat, but to-day I was told, on a visit there-and I think the member for Southeast Grey might go there-that they now have a
Supply-Agriculture

wheat which will perhaps supersede the Marquis and will be a better quality. If any person will go into the horticultural or fiori-cultural branch under Mr. McKee, when the chrysanthemums are in bloom, and see the John R. Booth chrysanthemum, brought into being by Mr. McKee there, and practically adopted by an American, it would be a surprise to him. But these people had to come back and admit that it was a Canadian production, and to-day it is on the market under the name of the John R. Booth. Perhaps people might see the Motherwell geranium or the Tolmie geranium, if they went there. These are all experiments that are bettering conditions in this country, and I think it ill-becomes any person to cast a slur on the experimental farm. I have under my hand here the catalogue of the horticultural wizard of the United States, Burbank. If we had a Burbank in this country, would it not be an advantage to us? We have men who have made developments along the line of floriculture and horticulture, and they should be encouraged, and my only regret is that larger amounts are not placed at the disposal of the farm and the government in order to carry on experiments.
In the fruit line we have had the development of apples. The country is not interested alone in wheat, there are other things in this country besides wheat, as hon. members will know if they visit the Niagara district. It would be a good idea if some of our western friends, who perhaps have not visited that section of the country, would come there and see what is going on. In direct opposition to the hon. member who has spoken tonight, I am a protectionist, and I have a constituent who is preparing now to put out forty acres of potatoes; he has them all sprouted. This time last year his potatoes were in the ground; I expect in another day or so they will be in the ground for this year. They try to get the early varieties in order to compete with-what?	To compete
with the vegetables from the South. And they are handicapped-no question about it. Everything that can be done to improve conditions should be done, and it is the duty of the experimental farm to develop the earliest and best kinds of fruit and vegetables. It is a great advantage to the growers in my district to know that by using the experimental farm either at Ottawa or Guelph they can receive great benefit, the experimenting, being done at the expense of the government.
I do not know if I am making a mistake, because the member for Southeast Grey

started to castigate this House for taking up too much time on this item. Well, it is an item of $1,500,000 and I think the time of the House is well taken up in discussing it, because a great many things have been brought out that will be of benefit to the province of Ontario and the Dominion of Canada. I think the experimental farms should be encouraged. It may be that there are overlappings, but I believe they have done a great work and everything we can do in this House to encourage agriculture, floriculture and horticulture should be done.

I agree with the last speaker that this is a very important item, and I do not know that the time taken this afternoon has been altogether rvasted. It is such an important matter that I think it should be brought to the attention of the House that there are only ten members of the Conservative group which sits to our right present to-night to see that this item is properly discussed. It may not be out of place to bring to your attention, Mr. Chairman, the fact that the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) is not in his place. I believe he has been called by some of the members the official timekeeper of the House, and I think it might be wise if we would continue the discussion a little longer, as possibly the timekeeper may be here when we take the vote. We have not gained as much information in regard to experimental farms as I think we should have obtained in the length of time we have been discussing this vote. I would like to bring to the attention of the chairman and members of the committee a little item in the Auditor General's report for 1923, which will show how some of the money voted for experimental farms is expended. On page 150 of the Auditor General's report I find the following:
Audit Office, Ottawa,
November 6, 1923.
Sir,-Included in the expenditure charged to experimental farms appropriation for the fiscal year 1922-23,
I find a number of payments made in connection with the entertainment of excursionists, etc.
Starting some years ago with a trifling outlay at Central Farm, Ottawa, this form of expenditure has extended to several of the branch farms, and now aggregates a considerable amount.
During the fiscal year 1922-23, outlay of this nature at Central Farm alone amounted to $1,115.68 and at Cap Rouge, Quebec, farm, to $836.68.
Such expenditure is not, in my opinion, properly chargeable to experimental farms appropriation, and should be incurred only after the special authority of parliament has been obtained therefor.
I would be very much obliged if the hon. minister, before we are asked to vote on this item, would tell us, if he knows, just how much has been expended for the purpose of

entertaining excursionists. On page 152 of this report I find a letter from the Auditor General to the deputy minister, dated 9th November, 1923, which says:
Included in the expenditure made from live stock appropriation in the fiscal year 1922-23, I find that by cheque No. 42837 the Chateau Laurier, Ottawa, received the sum of $202 covering the cost of a '' banquet on December 1, 1922, for members of the Live Stock branch."
The account is as follows:
70 dinners at $2.50	$175
Rather expensive dinners.
Not as they go now.

Well, for farmers. Then the next item reads:
Cigars and cigarettes	$ ft
Service	 10
I am just a little doubtful what kind of "service" that is. One of my hon. friends suggests that possibly it is liquid service. We ought to have a little more information regarding the expenditures included in this item. I hope the minister, before he asks us to vote on this question, will be good enough to tell us the amount he spent on each experimental farm last year. That will not take very long, and then the members who live near those farms will have some idea, possibly, whether the amount is being wisely expended or not.
I should like to draw the attention of the minister to one fact which has been mentioned here, but not stressed as, I think, it should be. I refer to the efforts of the Experimental Farms branch which, so far as I am aware, have been directed altogether to increasing production, and we have in Canada to-day, in a great many lines of agricultural produce, a surplus of production for the markets we have. Many authorities in the United States say that the American farmer raises too much wheat and that that is the reason why prices are so low. The Secretary of Agriculture in the Harding cabinet recently said:
Reduce the number of farmers, and the ones that are left will get more for their products.
I do not think the Minister of Agriculture whom we have in this cabinet, will agree with that, because last summer I believe he made the proud boast that Canada was now leading the world as a wheat exporter. I do not believe it is necessary for him to carry on experiments to any great extent at the present time for increasing production, particularly of wheat, because I have a little despatch from a Calgary paper which states:
On the provincial government farm at Olds last year they were able to produce 105 bushels of wheat to the acre.
The government statistics this year, I believe, state that the average yield of wheat in Alberta is 28 bushels to the acre, and I do not believe that record can be excelled by any country in the world. What the farmers need-and they do need some help-is some assistance in marketing this product. I want to quote from the Montreal Gazette of May 19 last. This statement was made by Col. Cooper, who was trade commissioner at New York during the war period. In referring to conditions in Canada, he said:
The marketing of our wheat was the crudest part of the whole foreign trade system, forcing our crop on the European market during three months, at a time when that market was flooded with wheat from all over the world, with the natural result of low prices. This meant a great deal for the industrial life of the country, because a poor price for wheat was bound to react on the purchasing price of the whole community.
I want to urge upon the minister that he should use his influence to see that there is returned to the wheat producers of the prairie provinces the amount of money which is now held by this government but which was left in their hands by the old wheat board now to be used for the purpose of assisting the farmers of the West in the formation of their wheat pools. I think he would be doing a much better service to the farmers of the West if he did that than he is in spending money to encourage them to produce more at the present time.
There is another matter which I want to bring to the attention of the minister, but I am not sure whether it is in order at this time or not. If it is not in order the minister can correct me. I have in my hand three different advertisements which were published in nearly all of the papers in Canada last year. I wish, Mr. Chairman, that I had time to read all these advertisements to you, because they are very entertaining. Each one of them winds up with the statement at the bottom in large black letters "Have faith in Canada". I believe these advertisements were accompanied by a little editorial; at least, this editorial was published in many of the papers that published the advertisements in question. One paragraph of this reads:
The farmer must remember that in the last analysis he is infinitely better off than the wage earner of the city.
I want to give the committee just a little idea of the comparison existing between what the farmer receives and what the labourer in the city receives. This is taken from the Farm and Ranch Review of Calgary, and I am sure the minister will consider it an authority. It states:
